lines.text: Five towns. Thousands of people lived in each one. Then, one day, they all left... and never came back. Tonight, partner, we're walking empty streets.
Nevada, near Death Valley. In 1905, two prospectors struck gold in the hills.
Within two weeks, about twelve hundred people had moved in. By 1907 there were thousands. Three railroads. An opera house. Electric streetlights.
The three story Cook Bank was finished in 1908. It cost more than ninety thousand dollars.
A miner named Tom Kelly built his house out of about fifty thousand bottles.
Then came the financial panic of 1907. The mines started closing. By 1910 the streetlights were switched off. In 1920, the census counted fourteen people.
California, high in the hills east of Yosemite. Bodie.
By 1879, thousands of people lived here, chasing gold, in around two thousand buildings.
The gold ran out. A fire in 1932 destroyed most of what was left. By the 1940s, the town was almost empty.
Since 1962 the state has kept Bodie just as it was found. Desks in the schoolhouse. Goods on the shelves. They call it arrested decay.
And there's a rule. Don't take anything. The park still receives packages of nails, bottles and rocks, sent back with letters from people who say the town cursed them.
Namibia, 1908. A railway worker named Zacharias Lewala was clearing sand from the tracks when he spotted a shiny stone.
It was a diamond. A German mining town rose out of the desert. Stone houses, a ballroom, a theatre, an ice factory, and a hospital with the first X-ray machine in the southern hemisphere.
Then richer diamond fields were found to the south. People left, many leaving their things behind. By 1956, Kolmanskop was empty.
And the desert came inside. Today, visitors walk through rooms filled to the windows with sand.
Off the coast of Nagasaki, Japan, there's an island that looks like a battleship.
Hashima. Mitsubishi bought it in 1890 to mine coal from under the sea, walled it in, and stacked concrete apartment blocks on top of it.
In 1959, five thousand two hundred and fifty nine people lived on sixteen acres. One of the most crowded places ever recorded.
Before and during the Second World War, Korean and Chinese laborers were brought here and forced to work in the mines.
In 1974 the mine closed. Within months, everyone was gone. Today, tour boats circle it, and visitors may walk only a small part of the island.
Northern Ukraine. Pripyat, built in 1970 for the workers of the Chernobyl nuclear plant. Nearly fifty thousand people lived here.
On April 26th, 1986, reactor number four exploded, about three kilometres away.
For more than a day, life went on. Then, on the afternoon of April 27th, the buses came. Residents were told to pack for three days.
They never came back.
The Ferris wheel had been due to open on May first, for the holiday. It never officially turned. The bumper cars are still where they stopped.
Today, Pripyat is still empty.
Five towns. Five ways a whole town can just... stop. Which one would you walk through alone? Tell me in the comments. Subscribe for more files. I'll be waiting, partner.
